newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S. Korean unions scale down strikes, clashes erupt.
newsitem.headline: S. Korean unions scale down strikes, clashes erupt.

text.p: South Korean strike leaders on Saturday abandoned calls for indefinite stoppages in protest at a controversial labour law as riot police clashed violently with workers in the streets of central Seoul.

Separately, police arrested a shipyard unionist in the southeastern city of Ulsan, bringing to five the number of union heads picked up since South Korean courts last week issued warrants for the arrest of 20 labour leaders.
In a sign union bosses were wilting under pressure, the leader of the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions said its members would limit industrial action.
But a brief clash between riot police and 4,000 workers and students showed passions were still inflamed over the law, which allows companies to dismiss workers and replace strikers.
"From next week, full strikes will take place only on Wednesday. On other weekdays, union members will work normally," Kwon Young-kil told a news conference.
Kwon warned of an "all-out struggle" from February 18 unless the government promised to revise the labour law.
Kwon and six deputies, who have led more than three weeks of stoppages that have now largely tapered off, are sheltering from arrest at Myongdong Cathedral in central Seoul.

Police vehicles fired volleys of teargas at the 4,000 protesters following a noisy rally in what has become a regular sight in Seoul since the law was rammed through parliament at dawn on December 26 while opposition deputies slept.
The protesters, trying to march on Myongdong some four km (2.5 miles) away, fought back with iron rods and ripped up paving stones to hurl at police before being dispersed.
Later, hundreds regrouped in shopping alleyways near the cathedral and fought running battles with riot police. The clashes ended after less than an hour.
The government has heaped pressure on the confederation fugitives, keeping a tight security noose around the church, preventing union activists from getting in or out.
In Ulsan, police arrested Kim Il-shik, confederation leader of Hyundai Heavy Industries, the country's largest shipyard, in an early morning raid.
Police said Kim was charged with obstructing business.

Earlier this week four union officials from Halla Heavy Industries were arrested on similar charges. State prosecutors have warned the strike leaders they faced arrest unless they dropped industrial action immediately.
An aide to Kwon said the confederation was changing tactics to prolong the protests, aiming more at a political struggle.
"If it is impossible to force this government to revise the law then we will have to oust it in the next election and seek a revision by a new ruling camp," he said.
South Korea is due to hold presidential elections in December. President Kim Young-sam is limited to one term.
Kim's popularity has plunged since his ruling New Korea Party railroaded the labour bill through parliament.
He has refused to revise or revoke the law, arguing that labour reform is crucial to trim corporate costs and improve international competitiveness.
Seizing on public dismay at the forced passage of the law, the opposition has thrown its weight behind union leaders.
Groups of opposition politicians, including main leader Kim Dae-jung and a number of parliamentarians, collected signatures in Seoul on Saturday to demand the government repeal the law.
Labour ministry officials said on Saturday the strikes had faded. The ministry said some 30,000 workers were on strike.
The confederation provided no comparative turnout.
Highlighting that only pockets of resistance remain, Hyundai Motor Co Ltd, the nation's largest carmaker, reopened on Saturday after a week of temporary shutdowns.
